planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; false bugbane is native to seepage slopes and streambanks and performs best in a consistently moist, boggy spot such as a rain garden or the edge of a shaded pond.

Trautvetteria caroliniensis is an eastern and western North American native with large, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves and airy clusters of fluffy white flowers made up of showy stamens rather than petals, blooming in late spring to early summer above the bold foliage. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a colony in consistently damp shade, providing a coarse, textural contrast to ferns and fine-leaved sedges along a shaded stream bank or wet woodland garden. Give it constant moisture — it does not tolerate summer drought — and full to partial shade, since foliage scorches quickly in hot sun or dry soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; trillium-leaf foamflower is native to moist Pacific Northwest conifer forests and, like other foamflowers, spreads gradually to form an attractive shaded groundcover.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; trillium-leaf foamflower is native to moist Pacific Northwest conifer forests and, like other foamflowers, spreads gradually to form an attractive shaded groundcover. Tiarella trifoliata differs from the familiar eastern Tiarella cordifolia in its distinctly three-parted, trillium-like leaflets rather than a single lobed leaf, with slender, airy spikes of small white to pale pink starry flowers rising above the foliage in late spring and early summer. It forms loose colonies in consistently moist, humus-rich forest soil, making it a good textural companion for ferns, vanilla leaf, and other Pacific Northwest woodland natives in a shaded garden. Keep soil evenly moist and mulched with leaf litter, and divide congested clumps in fall to propagate or maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; blackcap fruits on second-year canes, so tip-prune first-year primocanes in summer to encourage branching and next year's crop.

Rubus leucodermis is a western North American native bramble with arching, prickly canes coated in a whitish, waxy bloom, producing small white flowers in spring followed by dark purple-black, dome-shaped berries in early to midsummer that are tart, seedy, and excellent for jam, syrup, and baking. It tolerates lighter, drier soils and more shade than most cultivated raspberries, and its thicket-forming habit makes it useful for naturalized plantings, wildlife hedgerows, and erosion control on slopes as well as a home fruit patch. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting each year to keep the planting productive and manage its spreading habit.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; blue bean shrub needs a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for reliable pod set and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh drying wind.

Decaisnea insignis is a striking, large, multi-stemmed shrub from the Himalaya and western China with big, compound, tropical-looking leaves and drooping clusters of small yellow-green flowers in late spring, followed by the plant's signature feature — dangling, metallic blue, sausage-shaped seed pods in fall that give rise to its unsettling common name. The pods split open to reveal a translucent, gelatinous, mildly sweet pulp around black seeds that can be eaten fresh, similar in texture and flavor to a mild melon, though it is grown mostly as a conversation-piece ornamental rather than a serious food crop. It prefers a woodland-edge setting with shelter from wind and consistent moisture, and its architectural form and unusual fruit make it a standout specimen in a shaded border.
